column1: # Agents set to run commands without asking. One line each, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   agent     as the report shows it
#   os        all, mac, linux or win (win is Git Bash and gird-check.ps1)
#   path      the settings file, with the path tokens data/sessions.tsv uses, or {PROJECT}/folder/file
#             for that file in every project folder the home scan finds
#   setting   as the report shows it
#   pattern   one or more, each in its own field, and every one must match. Spaces are ignored. A
#             .json file is read as one line (the scripts' flat): a match starts at the text, a { or
#             a , and ends at the text's end, a , } # or /, so a longer key or another value never
#             counts. A pattern written "key": {... matches its rest that way, and only directly
#             inside the object that top-level key holds. A .toml file is read line by line: a line
#             starting with # is skipped, a match is a whole line (up to a # comment), so a setting
#             inside an inline table does not count, a value in double quotes also matches the same
#             value in single quotes (a TOML literal string), and only the lines before the first
#             [table] count (a setting under [profiles.x] applies only when that profile is used, and
#             Codex 0.134.0 and later read no such table from config.toml)
# Claude Code: code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes, and its settings reference, where defaultMode
# is a key of permissions and of nothing else. Codex: its configuration reference, and its
# advanced configuration page for profiles (0.134.0). TOML's literal strings: toml.io. VS Code:
# the Copilot settings reference and the 1.104 release notes. VS Code 1.104 renamed chat.tools.autoApprove
# to chat.tools.global.autoApprove without migrating it, so the old name is ignored, and it reads the
# new one from the user settings only (scope APPLICATION_MACHINE in its source), never from a
# project's .vscode/settings.json. A project's chat.tools.autoApprove is the setting CVE-2025-53773
# wrote; section 2 of the scripts lists it as a sign of that attack, not as a setting in force.
# VS Code added chat.permissions.default, the permission level new chats start with: autoApprove
# ("Allow all") and autopilot run every tool call without asking (VS Code's AI settings reference and
# approvals page; the values from chat.shared.contribution.ts). It declares no scope, and VS Code reads
# its merged value, so a project's .vscode/settings.json sets it too: section 2 of the scripts lists
# such a project's copy, as a setting a cloned project brings, not as a line here.
# chat.defaultConfiguration, an object whose approvals and mode would have to be read inside it, is
# not read.
